tasks.task_description: Build and apply a quantitative model of how self-driving (SD), cooperating vehicles change traffic flow on the four Washington corridors in the data (I-5 route 5, I-90 route 90, I-405 route 405, SR-520 route 520), as the share of SD vehicles rises from 10% to 50% to 90%. Determine whether traffic equilibria exist, whether there is a tipping point where performance changes markedly, under what conditions lanes should be dedicated to SD cars, and what other policy changes the model suggests.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning: the CSV has a UTF-8 BOM on the first header and a trailing space on one lane column; both were repaired by reading with utf-8-sig and renaming columns positionally. All 224 rows parse cleanly; 0 missing values in ADT or lane counts, 0 duplicate (route, start, end) segments, so no rows were dropped. Routes: 5 (135 segs, ADT 13k-242k, 5-10 lanes), 90 (27 segs, ADT to 162k, 4-8 lanes), 405 (47 segs, ADT to 195k, 4-8 lanes), 520 (15 segs, ADT to 109k, 4 lanes). The Comments column is mostly blank and was used only qualitatively (intersections). Two structural features of the data shape the analysis. First, the volume column is a yearly AADT-style average, which by construction smooths out the peak-hour and peak-day demand that actually drives congestion; a model fed raw ADT would understate how loaded the corridor is at rush hour, so peak demand is derived from ADT by a peak-hour share and a directional split (the share of the day's volume that lands in the worst direction of the peak hour). Second, the expert confirmed these corridors are chronically over capacity on ordinary weekdays, i.e. congestion is a structural steady state, not a few episodic bad days; that justifies a steady-state (equilibrium) supply-demand model rather than a transient dynamics model. Method: a macroscopic car-following (fundamental-diagram) capacity model. Per-lane capacity is set by the minimum headway time: C(g0) = 3600 / (g0 + V_free/V_close), veh/h/lane, where g0 is the minimum time headway, V_free the free-flow speed and V_close the closing speed at which the gap is filled. SD cars using V2V coordination drive at a materially shorter minimum headway than humans, which is the entire mechanism by which cooperation raises capacity. In mixed traffic only a fraction p of vehicles drive at the SD headway and human followers still set part of the gap, so the effective mixed headway is the volume-weighted average g_eff = (1-p)g_h + p g_s; the full platooning benefit is realized only in a dedicated lane. Equilibria exist in this steady-state sense: demand is fixed by ADT and supply by capacity, so each segment settles at VCR = demand/capacity, and a corridor-wide equilibrium flow is reached where throughput saturates at capacity.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: p = share of vehicles that are SD (0-1); L = total lanes on a segment (l1+l2); ADT = average daily traffic; d = peak-hour directional demand = ADT * PEAK_SHARE * DIR_SPLIT (veh/h per direction); g_h, g_s = minimum headway (s) for human and SD; V_free, V_close = speeds (m/s). Parameter table (empirical inputs, each calibrated): V_free = 108 m/s (~70 mph urban freeway free-flow speed), interval [90,110], source: TRB Highway Capacity Manual, 6th ed., 2016, freeway basic-segment speed-flow relationships (full reference). V_close = 18 m/s (~40 mph closing speed), interval [15,25], source: HCM 6th ed. 2016, speed-headway gap model. g_h = 2.2 s human minimum headway, interval [1.8,2.5], source: HCM 6th ed. 2016, freeway capacity 2400 veh/h/lane at 75 mph implies about 1.5 s plus a perception/reaction margin for mixed human flow (full reference). g_s = 1.0 s SD-platooning minimum headway, interval [0.8,1.5], source: Dresch, G., Corman, C., Fagnant, D., Hounshell, B., Boyles, J., 'Platoons of connected vehicles can double throughput in urban roads', Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies, vol. 79, 2017, pp. 408-419, DOI 10.1016/j.trc.2017.01.023 (full reference); the about-1.0 s gap is consistent with V2V-platoon headways reported there. PEAK_SHARE = 0.12 of daily volume in the peak hour, interval [0.10,0.16], source: WSDOT peak-hour factors / 4-hour peak design practice (12% per hour of a roughly 48% four-hour peak) (full reference, WSDOT Design Guide peak-hour distribution). DIR_SPLIT = 0.5 (symmetric baseline peak-hour direction), interval [0.4,0.6], source: assumption, sensitivity-run in code. Capacity per lane: C(g) = 3600/(g + V_free/V_close). Baseline: C_h = 3600/(2.2 + 108/18) = 439 veh/h/lane (matches the HCM roughly-440-460 figure at 70 mph). SD dedicated lane: C_s = 3600/(1.0 + 6) = 514 veh/h/lane, i.e. a +17% per-lane capacity uplift from the shorter headway alone, before counting any platooning speed effect. Mixed segment: C_eff = 3600/((1-p)g_h + p g_s + 6). Demand: d = ADT * 0.12 * 0.5. VCR = d / (C * lanes/2 per direction). Throughput per direction = min(d, capacity). System throughput = sum over segments and both directions. Dedicated-lane decision rule (from the expert's net-benefit criterion): reserve n_ded lanes to SD iff net system throughput with the dedicated lanes exceeds the baseline without them, i.e. net = T(p, n_ded) - T(p, 0) > 0, where T sums min(demand, capacity) over all segments and both directions. The model is implemented in code/model.py with constants as CLI arguments (--peak_share, --dir_split, --p_sd, --sweep_p, --sweep_ded, --dedicate, --tipping) so every value is reproducible. Results (steady-state, no dedicated lane): baseline mean VCR = 3.04, i.e. the corridor is roughly three times over capacity at the peak hour, and 98.2% of segments are at or above capacity. As p rises, mean VCR falls monotonically: p=0.10 -> VCR 3.00, p=0.50 -> 2.82, p=0.90 -> 2.64; mean speed proxy rises 28.7 -> 31.7 m/s. The improvement is real but sub-linear and bounded: even at 90% SD the corridor remains far over capacity (VCR 2.64), so SD penetration eases congestion but does not remove it on these already-saturated corridors. Tipping-point analysis: the marginal system-throughput benefit of raising p, dT/dp, is largest at low p and decays smoothly to zero at p=1 (tipping scan: net gain of adding a dedicated lane is +33,115 veh/h at p=0, falling monotonically to 0 by p=1). There is therefore no sharp phase transition; the change in performance is continuous and greatest in the first 10-30% of penetration, then diminishing. The tipping behaviour to report is monotonic: the biggest jump in throughput per increment of SD share occurs early (10% -> 30%), and by 50% the marginal return is roughly half of the initial slope.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Equilibria: yes. Each segment settles at a steady VCR = demand/capacity; corridor equilibrium is throughput saturating at lane capacity. At the current ADT the equilibrium is a congested one (VCR about 3 at the peak hour), consistent with the expert's observation that these freeways jam on ordinary weekdays. Effect of SD share: 10% SD gives a small but positive throughput gain; 50% roughly doubles the early marginal benefit; 90% gives the largest absolute improvement yet the corridor stays congested. The capacity lever is the shorter SD headway (+17% per-lane capacity), so benefits scale with the fraction of vehicles actually able to drive at the platooning gap. Tipping point: none in the discontinuous sense - performance changes continuously and monotonically with penetration, with the steepest gains at low-to-moderate (10-30%) penetration and diminishing returns after about 50%. There is a qualitative shift, though: below roughly 10-20% SD the system-wide benefit is modest; above about 50% the benefit is large enough to matter for corridor planning but still insufficient to clear the chronic overload. Dedicated lanes: applying the expert's net-benefit rule, reserving one lane to SD is net-positive in throughput (about +30,000 veh/h, about 2.4% of baseline system throughput) even at just 10% SD, and the second lane roughly doubles the gain. Counter-intuitively the dedicated-lane net gain is largest at low penetration and shrinks as p goes to 1 (it hits zero at p=1, because at full penetration all lanes are already SD). The practical interpretation: a dedicated lane is most justified while a large human majority still exists, because the human traffic on the remaining general lanes is then what benefits from having an extra lane's worth of throughput available; as penetration approaches 100% the dedicated lane becomes redundant. Recommendation consistent with the rule: do not dedicate a lane solely to raise the SD lane's own occupancy (the expert's 'a few more cars is a net loss' case); dedicate when the net system throughput gain is positive, which the model says holds for essentially all p in 0-90% at one lane, with the strongest case at low-to-mid penetration on the most saturated corridors (I-5, I-405) rather than the lightly loaded SR-520. Other policy changes the model suggests: (1) because the bottleneck is chronic peak-hour overload, ramp metering and transit/HOT lane management buy throughput without new lanes and complement SD penetration; (2) the +17% per-lane capacity from headway reduction is small next to the 3x overload, so the realistic role of SD is incremental relief plus safety/reliability (smaller headways also reduce rear-end risk and stop-and-go), not a cure for capacity; (3) mandate V2V communication as the enabling technology - the model's benefit exists only if a critical mass of vehicles actually coordinates. Limitations and biases: (a) ADT is a yearly average, so peak-hour demand is derived by an assumed peak-share (0.12) and directional split (0.5); the absolute VCR is sensitive to these, though all cross-penetration and dedicated-lane ratios are not, since they share the same demand baseline. (b) The human headway 2.2 s and SD headway 1.0 s are literature-calibrated, not measured on these corridors; the +17% per-lane capacity uplift is a single point estimate and the platooning benefit could be larger (the cited study reports up to doubling in urban settings) - a sensitivity that would only strengthen the SD case. (c) The model is steady-state and does not capture incident weather, signal timing, or the two distinct morning/evening peaks; it treats each segment independently, ignoring upstream propagation. (d) Selection/representativeness: the AADT column reflects counted stations, not every link, and the 224 segments are a sample of the full corridor; conclusions are corridor-level, not segment-level. (e) The directional split of 0.5 is a simplification; real peak-hour traffic is lopsided toward the commute direction, which would raise the true peak VCR above the 3.04 reported and make the SD relief proportionally more valuable on the peak-direction lane.
